title: Coded Clifford Measurements for Multiqubit Magic-State Cultivation
abstract: Magic-state cultivation suppresses errors by measuring logical Clifford symmetries and discarding inconsistent outcomes. For an entangled resource several branches are accepted, so the retained branch carries a multibit classical record whose corruption produces a logical-frame error. We show that this record layer is exactly a binary linear code. For any third-level Clifford-hierarchy unitary $U \in \mathcal{C}_3$, the branches $UZ(a)|+\rangle^{\otimes k}$ are resolved by commuting Hermitian Clifford observables $C(v) = UX(v)U^{\dagger}$, so a measurement schedule is a generator matrix and postselection on valid records gives $P_{\mathrm{wv}} = O(q^{d})$ at record distance $d$. A Plotkin bound then limits every binary record, linear or not. The physically realizable Clifford family already saturates it: at distance four, six logical measurements suffice for $|CS\rangle$ and seven for $|CCZ\rangle$, against eight and twelve for independent repetition. Restricting to fault-tolerantly measurable parities therefore costs nothing in record length. The saving survives compilation: in a native-CZZ-assisted Steane realization the $[6,2,4]$ CS schedule is the unique minimum-cost distance-four solution, reducing the cultivation core by 26.6\% in active locations, and exact state-vector simulation without a final ideal code-space projection confirms higher acceptance and roughly half the residual Steane-boundary weight. Coding thus reduces logical redundancy and compiled overhead together.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework showing how coding theory can be used to protect the measurement record during magic-state cultivation for fault-tolerant quantum computation. By mapping error detection to linear codes, the authors demonstrate that the required physical resources are significantly reduced compared to naive repetition schemes. This provides a pathway for building more resource-efficient quantum circuits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for efficient, fault-tolerant methods to cultivate magic quantum states required for computation by measuring logical Clifford symmetries.
main_result: Coded Clifford measurements provide a resource-efficient way to protect the measurement record, achieving significant reductions in required physical resources compared to independent repetition schemes.
method: The authors map the error detection problem onto the theory of binary linear codes, using commuting Hermitian Clifford observables to define the measurement schedule via a generator matrix.
model_or_system: The model involves multiqubit magic-state cultivation, where the error protection is encoded in the classical record derived from measuring logical Clifford symmetries ($C(\mathbf{v})$) associated with third-level Clifford-hierarchy unitaries ($U \in \mathcal{C}_3$).
key_observables: Code distance ($d_G$), active locations, qubit-steps, and the error probability scaling $P_{wv} = O(q^{d_G})$.
important_parameters: Target distance $d=4$, resource reduction percentages (e.g., 26.6% reduction in active locations).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a specific noise model for the record layer and distinguishes between algebraically available logical gates and physically fault-tolerant implementations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the logical-level code–cultivation correspondence, quantifying resource reductions (e.g., 28.3% gate-step reduction) for distance four coding, and showing the minimum length of the $[7, 3, 4]$ simplex record.
paper_structure: The paper develops the logical-level code–cultivation correspondence, derives the necessary observables $C(\mathbf{v})$, establishes the code-theoretic bounds (Plotkin bound), and finally optimizes the minimum-cost schedule by solving an integer covering problem.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous application of coding theory to physical measurement constraints provides a powerful mathematical framework applicable to any physical system where measurement outcomes must be robustly correlated.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Logical-level code–cultivation correspondence. A third-level resource basis provides commuting Clifford checks C(v). Choosing check labels vt defines the measurement schedule G = [v1 · · · vn] and the valid record code RG = {aG}. Postselection accepts only valid records; a wrong accepted branch therefore requires a nonzero displacement e ∈RG, so the record-code distance dG sets the accepted record-error order, Pwv = O(qdG).

FIG. 2. Consequences of coded Clifford records. (a) For distance four, coding reduces the CS schedule from 8 to 6 logical checks, from 948 to 696 compiled-core active locations, and from 2844 to 2040 active-qubit gate steps; the CCZ schedule falls from 12 to 7 logical checks. (b) The optimal [5, 2, 3] and [6, 2, 4] two-bit records give cubic and quartic wrong-acceptance scaling. (c) The [7, 3, 4] CCZ simplex schedule reaches the minimum length allowed for any binary record.
FIG. 1. Exact semantics of one logical record measurement. The circuit realizes the projectors in Eq. (48); it is an algebraic reference circuit, not a claim of low fault-tolerant overhead.

FIG. 2. Live Steane-boundary diagnostics after removing the final ideal code-space projection. Left: record-and-midpoint acceptance. Right: mean weight of the canonical two-block Steane boundary representative among accepted shots. Error bars show one standard error. These are boundary-quality diagnostics, not full-factory logical-error estimates.
